questions.question: Why does the hour hand's continuous movement (not jumping instantly at each hour) matter for angle calculations?
options: Because the hour hand moves gradually between hour marks, so its exact position depends on the minutes as well as the hour
It doesn't matter, the hour hand only matters at exact hours
Because the hour hand is actually stationary
Because only the minute hand's position matters for angle calculations
questions.rationale: The hour hand drifts 0.5 degrees per minute between hour marks, so an accurate angle calculation must account for the current minutes, not just the hour.

questions.question: How many degrees per second does the second hand move?
options: 1 degree
3 degrees
6 degrees
12 degrees
questions.rationale: The second hand completes 360 degrees in 60 seconds, so it moves 360/60 = 6 degrees per second — the same rate the minute hand moves per minute.

questions.question: At approximately what time (in minutes past 12) do the minute and hour hands first overlap after 12:00?
options: Exactly 60 minutes
Approximately 65 5/11 minutes
Exactly 30 minutes
Approximately 72 minutes
questions.rationale: The hands overlap roughly every 65 5/11 minutes, since the minute hand must 'catch up' the extra distance the slower-moving hour hand covers in the meantime.

questions.question: What does a 'temporal relationship' describe in clock reasoning?
options: The color of the clock face
Only the numeric difference between two times
The manufacturer of the clock
How two events or times relate to each other — before, after, simultaneous, or overlapping
questions.rationale: A temporal relationship describes the qualitative connection between two events or times, such as whether one precedes, follows, or overlaps with the other.

questions.question: What defines a 'time interval'?
options: A start time and an end time defining a duration
A single point in time
Only the duration, with no start or end
A recurring event with no fixed length
questions.rationale: A time interval is defined by its start and end times, together specifying a duration between two points.

questions.question: When do two time intervals 'overlap'?
options: Only when they start at exactly the same time
Only when one interval fully contains the other
When one interval's start is before the other's end, and vice versa — they share some common time
Intervals can never overlap by definition
questions.rationale: Two intervals overlap whenever each one's start time is before the other's end time, meaning there is some shared span of time between them.

questions.question: What is the goal of 'scheduling reasoning' in this context?
options: Drawing a calendar
Determining whether events can be arranged without time conflicts, given their intervals
Calculating clock-hand angles
Converting between 12-hour and 24-hour format
questions.rationale: Scheduling reasoning uses interval overlap logic to determine whether a set of events can coexist without conflicting for the same time slot.

questions.question: What does 'relative time' refer to, as opposed to an absolute clock time?
options: A time defined in relation to another event (e.g., '10 minutes after the meeting starts') rather than a fixed clock value
A time that changes randomly
A time zone-adjusted value
A synonym for elapsed time
questions.rationale: Relative time expresses a moment in terms of its relationship to another event or reference point, rather than as a fixed, standalone clock value.

questions.question: What is a 'temporal chain'?
options: A physical chain used on grandfather clocks
A sequence of events or times linked by relative time relationships (e.g., A happens, then B 20 minutes later, then C...)
A list of unrelated random times
A synonym for a single time interval
questions.rationale: A temporal chain links a sequence of events through relative time relationships, where each event's time depends on the one before it.

questions.question: Why is representing temporal relationships explicitly (rather than just as a list of separate times) useful?
options: It isn't useful — a plain list is always sufficient
It preserves the dependencies between events, letting you correctly propagate a change in one time through the rest of the chain
It removes the need for the clock-angle formula
It only matters for events on different days
questions.rationale: Explicit relationships preserve how events depend on each other, so if one time shifts, the correct downstream effect on the rest of the chain can be recalculated.
